The emergence of communications media in the USA
As the value of offering products to mass markets was recognized in the USA in he early
20th century, industries for communicating information to mass audiences emerged.
Newspapers had been present in North America since the 18th century, but now, - ie

business life. Newspapers and advertising agencies had a common emphasis that
distinguished them from other enterprises: the product they sold was information. The
development of new entrepreneurial activities was greatly facilitated by technical
improvements in transportation and mass communication. As the railroad, telegraph, and
telephone reduced communication distances, and printing presses became more efficient,
newspapers and advertisers could reach more customers.
In the 1920s, with the commercialization of radio, another communications industry emerged.
Originally developed by the armed forces to transmit messages in wartime, wireless sets
were adapted to household use, and the first commercial radio stations came into being.
Anyone could enter the radio industry by obtaining a license from the federal government —
but problems surfaced. One was the phenomenon of ‘spectrum interference’ by signals of
radio stations located close to one another on the available broadcast spectrum. In the
evening hours, atmospheric conditions meant that interference from out-of-town stations was
a problem in areas where local stations were broadcasting. The federal government, which
claimed jurisdiction over the airwaves, recognized that broadcast frequencies needed to be
assigned, rather than chosen at random by license-holders.
A further problem was with the content of radio broadcasts. Programs often featured
advertisements and outspoken views on controversial topics. Some advertisements
appeared to be misleading, and some attitudes expressed by commentators on stations were
offensive to certain groups. In 1927, Congress created the Federal Radio Commission
(FRC), whose powers included the assignment of frequencies and the regulation of content.
In 1934, it was replaced by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), which initially
was strongly biased in favor of ‘highbrow’ programming, featuring classical music concerts
and public affairs programs.

Then came television. The decade of the 1950s was to television as the 1920s was to radio:
by 1960 more than 80 percent of American households owned a TV set. Television
programming initially mirrored that of radio: the FCC encouraged networks to run a
combination of network shows, generated from one source, and local news and public affairs
shows. It distributed TV licenses and controlled the process by which they were renewed.
Initially, the television broadcast spectrum was limited to ‘very high frequency’ (VHF)
channels in a narrow band. The narrow spectrum meant the market for television franchises
was limited, so owning a television station could be very lucrative. From their origins, radio
and television stations were ‘free’ to listeners or viewers (apart from the cost of acquiring a
set). Station operators made their money from advertising.
In 1952, recognizing the growing demand for television programs, the FCC authorized
broadcasting on ‘ultra high frequency’ (UHF) channels, which could send out signals on a
broader spectrum. These signals were more powerful than VHF ones but could not travel
very far, so they were more suitable for urban areas containing big populations. The FCC
anticipated that the UHF market would quickly result in more diverse programming, but this
did not occur, for two reasons. First, the signals of UHF stations were difficult to pick up
outside their immediate broadcast area, and UHF stations could not rely on networks to
duplicate their programs elsewhere. Second, UHF stations needed to develop all their own
programming, which meant that unless they achieved a niche in the television market, they
would have difficulty recovering the costs of program creation. Many UHF stations turned to
sports events. Such programming was less costly to produce and could be directed primarily
at local markets.
Few of the UHF channels allocated were therefore filled. Instead, in order to improve
reception in remote areas, communities began erecting antennas at high spots and running
signals from them by coaxial cables. The use of cables ensured that signal quality remained
good, but cable operators typically needed to secure licenses from municipal governments
for running them. Eventually, a system of cable franchising, controlled by cities and towns,
sprang up throughout the country. Unlike network television, cable television was sold
directly to consumers in the form of packages often including large numbers of channels,
both VHF and UHF. However, because cable providers typically had little competition in a
particular area, they were free to charge what the market would bear. The rest, it might be
said, is history.
